narrative:
The model predicts you have a 16% chance of failing your final year, which is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this decision were your number of past failures, your ambition to pursue higher education, and your record of school absences. Surprisingly, the strongest influence came from your clean record of zero past class failures. While this is identical to the average among students who passed, the model interpreted the absence of prior setbacks as unexpectedly increasing your risk in this specific case. Your clear desire to continue into higher education worked in your favor and pushed the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was outweighed by your 22 absences—far above the average of fewer than 4 days among students who successfully passed. These frequent absences proved to be a major negative factor, pulling the outcome toward failure.

Because the risk, although modest, exceeds the school’s safety threshold, remedial courses are now mandatory. To turn this around, focus first on dramatically improving your attendance. Consistent presence in class will likely have the biggest impact on your actual results. Protect the motivation you already have for higher education and build steady study habits around it. Small, regular improvements in showing up and keeping up with work can quickly shift your trajectory from borderline to secure.
